newsitem.title: USA: Green groups pressure Gore to back air rule.
newsitem.headline: Green groups pressure Gore to back air rule.

text.p: Environmental groups Tuesday stepped up pressure on Vice President Al Gore to come out in support of proposed tougher air quality standards, while congressional Democrats remained split on the issue.
"This is the Sierra Club's 'Where's Al?' tour," Kathryn Hohmann, of the environmental group, said in a telephone interview from New Hampshire.

A number of health and environmental activists were in New England this week to try to increase pressure on Gore, usually their ally, to publicly support the Environmental Protection Agency's proposal to tighten standards against smog and soot.

Gore has not commented on the proposal, which has drawn fire from many industry and local government interests and which is under intensive review by the White House's National Economic Council and its Council on Environmental Quality.

A spokesman for the vice president said he would hold off on commenting until the White House makes a decision on the controversial proposal, which sources said could come as early as this week or next week.
Hohmann said it was not coincidental that the tour passed through New Hampshire, site of the first presidential primary and a factor in Gore's presidential hopes.

"We're here to say 'come out, come out wherever you are,'" Hohmann said. "Our goal is not to bash someone, but there are some very large shoes he needs to fill" in leading environmental causes, she said.
The environmental groups were focusing on the Northeast, where the EPA's proposal has the strongest support.
But the EPA proposal has drawn fire from many other parts of the country, has heavy Republican opposition, and is pitting Democrats against Democrats.
Emerging from a policy session, key Senate Democrats said they were divided on the issue.

"There's no consensus in our caucus, obviously," said John Breaux, of Louisiana, who joined forces with Rhode Island Republican Sen. John Chafee to push the administration to delay the stronger standards.
Chafee and Breaux were circulating a letter calling on the EPA to set an equivalent standard for smog, but averaged more than eight hours instead of the current one hour.

They urged the White House to hold off on setting a new standard for soot, or tiny particulate matter of less than 2.5 microns in diameter, because the EPA proposal "is not supported by the best science."
The senators said a new standard for the fine particles should be warranted only if epidemiologial studies, backed by studies in exposure chambers, showed a clearly defined risk.
But critics said that plan would strip the EPA's authority to protect public health and create new barriers to regulations.
"I view it as asking the administration to not follow the law," Sen. Joseph Lieberman, a Connecticut Democrat, said.
He and Sen. Max Baucus, a Montana Democrat, were circulating letters backing the EPA's proposal.
